Interview of
GEORGE HANDY
March, 1980

INTERVIEWER:
Bill Schremp

S. & S. REPORTING CO., INC.
Court Reporters—Notaries
132 Nassau Street
New York City
2915
WOrth 2-2943

I will sort of prompt you and push you along and ask questions and try not to put my priceless opinions in here, although it is very difficult for me to keep out of an interview; it's one of my terrible habits.
It's not a bad habit.
Anyway, we're back in Brooklyn.
Did I live in Brooklyn?
Weren't you born in Brooklyn?
I was born in Brooklyn, yes, but you want to know about my early life? You wanted to know about the beginning of Raeburn; didn't you?
No, this is George Handy. This has nothing to do with Raeburn. This is George Handy.
I'm in Brooklyn, smelling ether all day long, from morning till night. My father was a doctor and he performed-- what do you call it--the ear operations--mastoids,
That was the genesis of that title.
Yeah, well--tonsillectomy, out of respect for my father, to actually let him know he was a part of my thoughts in my music somewhere, so I titled it 'Tonsillectomy'.
Lorraine said you referred to him as the 'tonsil doctor'?
Did I?
In the book.
Yeah, he was, they used to line up to have their throats cut by my father.
Anyway, the apartment smelled of ether, it got so I could live in a world of ether without being affected by it.
That was in the beginning, and then we moved upstairs and I didn't escape from the ether, it seeped through the ceiling into where we were living.
That was my beginning.
Your mother was

My mother was a pianist, right. She was always preparing for a concert that never happened. She really didn't intend to have a concert, but she trained as if she would have. She practiced faithfully everyday, she would practice the same music on each day and we would have the same food--this is funny, because when I'd come home from school and I'd hear my mother practicing, I would know what I was going to have for lunch, according to what she was playing.
That lead to a well ordered life.
Well, reasonably ordered at that time.
Is that the piano she was playing then?
No, she had another-- let me think--this may well be that piano, and then again I don't know.
There may have been a change of
pianos when I was going to public school.
Was your father musical in any way?
No, he was an enjoyer, he wasn't musical. But he had good taste, surprisingly. I don't know why.
At what point did you get into this--were you given piano lessons or something like that?

My mother started to train me and she was an impossible teacher, she made it pure hell for me. I kicked a hole in the piano one day, ran out and that was the end of my musical training--at least by my mother. There was a real upheaval in the house at the time, my father and mother got into a big argument about me, and my father recognized that she was driving me out of my nut and he said let him up, let him do what he wants to, which was great for me, because I really wanted to get away from music. She really had made it a tortuous process for me. She used to shriek and scream if I did
You didn't stay away from it very long?
A few years I had nothing to do with music at all.
What brought you back?

I just wandered back by myself. I felt an urge to get back to it, but on my own terms. I suspect that the way she trained me in music was actually training me to resent being trained by other people. I resented every school I went to, every teacher I ever had. I stopped listening to my teachers; most of them didn't have too much to say actually. I really resented being told anything, I had to do it myself, I had to discover it myself, and that's the way it went.
Did you find a teacher who took advantage of that and worked with

No, it was always a battle. I never found a teacher that I enjoyed. While I'm saying this, I'm searching my mind, trying to think perhaps there was somebody; but not really, no. I had to do it by myself; I had to discover what was wrong by myself.
As I explained to you last night, through other musicians, they told me what I had done that was bad or wrong.
When you got back into music, did you do it in terms of your mother's music or were you at that point thinking in terms jazz or of /popular music or whatever?
I was just thinking in terms of being inventive, seeing what I could discover at the keyboard, seeing whether I could make sounds I never heard before, harmonic changes I never heard before.
Were you listening to other people then?
I was listening to

classical music mostly, the moderns. I was listening--discovering Stravinsky was a big thing for me. When I first heard his music I really flipped out. I loved the way he wrote. Then Ravel, Bartok. The moderns, at the beginning, were the people that really stirred me up, that really got me thinking.

As the years went by, I went backwards in terms of listening to composers. I got back to Bach, Beethoven, Mozart, and for the first time really appreciated them. But I had to hear the moderns first in order to appreciate the classics.
What was your first job playing? What was your first job, not playing?

It was the same job, and it was playing. I was about fourteen or fifteen and the family usually took a bungalow, or a house for the summer at Rockaway Beach, and I had a neighbor that lived across the street from me who was a saxophone player, and he came

over to the house one day and heard that I played the piano, told me that he had gotten a job in Long Beach at one of the hotels and he needed a pianist. Of course I wanted the job, I accepted it. My mother fought like all get out; she didn't want her son living anywhere else but at home, and this was a live away job.

But once again my father came to the rescue, said it was all right for me to do and I took the job. We worked the summer job in this hotel in Long Beach and it was a kid band, I don't recall that we played any--we might have had a show or two, I didn't read very well at the time, but I had good instinct so I was able to handle it.
You were playing things from sheet music and pop tunes and that sort of thing?
Yes, but I was following the cord structure in those days pretty much rather than reading note for note. That was the first job, playing with a drum, trumpet, piano
and saxophone. I don't think we had a bass.
Is there anybody that survived, were any of them later to become players?
I don't even--I only remember one fellow out of all of them, and he didn't remain a musician. I was the only one, as you say, survived. Musical survival.
Where did you go from there? This would be the early thirties; wouldn't it?
Yes; right.

From there I had an interest in playing with other guys, forming bands, and there was a period of finding other neighborhood musicians, kids that knew other kids that played instruments, trying to put together a little band.
You thought of yourself then as from now on a musician?
I might have had an idea that that's what I wanted to do. I don't think I made a firm commitment at that time. I had still been told by my father that I was going
to be a doctor and I didn't question any of this; I just assumed that I was going to be a doctor. That's what I was told I was going to be.
It didn't work out that way.
No. Dad was wrong.
He was on the right track. There are more doctors who are musicians than anybody else who are musicians. There's an entity between the two. I'm not sure what it is.
You're right; you're absolutely right. I've discovered that too.

As I said, I didn't make a commitment. I didn't know what I was going to do until the day my father took me with him to watch him perform an operation and I was over his shoulder wearing the white gown, the cap and the mask; really fascinated by it and he took out his scalpel and he cut behind the person's ear and peeled the flesh apart and I went backwards and down. When my father came out of the operation looking very pleased, 'How was that son, did you enjoy it?'
That's how jazz was born.
Period.
And your mother?
I don't think she was as disturbed as he was.
At this point were you conscious of learning problems, of having to work hard to get your chops together or did it come easily and natural?
Some of us--I should say some of you are blessed with never having to worry about
chops, always being able to play anything you could think of.
I don't think that's entirely true.

I have a facility--my word for it is bullshitting--I can manage to play as if I'm doing the right thing and it will sound to the whole world like it's the absolute proper thing and I'm not doing it at all, I'm doing something else, I'm just making it sound as if it's right.

It's like the time I was studying piano with some teacher and they gave a concert of students and I played a little thing by Mozart that had three movements in it and during the concert I completely forgot the second movement and ad libbed the second movement. I don't know how many people were fooled, but nobody said anything about the fact that I had altered or invented. I can do that with most music. I can get so close to what is supposed to be that people think it is. You can call that creative or inventive, but when I know that I'm not doing
That calls on the definition of what the right thing is.
What's written is the right thing.
Your whole force has been not to do what was written or indeed what was ordained, but whatever George Handy was looking for.

I think it all went back to my resentment of being taught. The whole structure offended me. Of course I think it's because of my mother's very neurotic approach to teaching. Sometimes it takes almost a lifetime to discover these things, they whys and then it's really too late to change anything. You just go along with what you've got and do your best.
Were you at that point doing composition and beginning to learn to write and thinking of writing?
I was doing it from the very beginning, and I think when I went back to
music after those few years away from it, probably the first thing I did was start to write.
For the kids bands and such or performance things for you, for piano?

I had an uncle that was a violinist, I would write violin and piano things because he would visit very often and we'd play together, or whatever was available to me, in terms of other musicians and what they played. I'd write for them.
How did your uncle feel about your work then? Presumably he was something of a traditionalist.
He was a pretty good egg. Excuse me. Where were we?
Your uncle's response to what you were writing. He was obviously used to playing printed music from Schirmer or something.
He handled it well.

The things I wrote he handled very well. What I meant to imply, he wasn't like my mother or my aunt who used to tell me I was the greatest thing that ever lived, which I couldn't take, it turned my stomach. My uncle was cool. He didn't praise me, but I could tell by the way he worked with me that what I was doing was acceptable to him on a professional level. That was all I needed. That was enough reassurance, which was genuine.
The compliments that I got from the rest of my family weren't genuine.
Was your entrance at Julliard your first formal music school?
First formal music school? Yeah; right.
You were primarily a composition student as opposed to an instrumentalist or did they make the distinction?
I had a few courses there, but Julliard wasn't a good experience for me either. I went to the movies most of the

time instead of going to school.
I listened to my instructors at the
beginning but didn't feel any rapport, didn't
feel anything from them, so I gave up quickly.
I dodged around.

You didn't get involved in the student activities there, the
student's bands or anything?
No.

Playing duets with
each other and that sort of nonsense?

I didn't find anybody
there that was interested in what I was interested
in. They were serious, classical students.

I remember trying to play some jazz
in one of the practice rooms and a whole bunch of
them--who the hell is that, who's that? What are
you doing, what are you playing? Like I was
committing a sacrilege, playing jazz in Julliard.
It was a bad experience.

How long were you
there?
A year. In that year, maybe two weeks. Maybe longer, but I wasn't a good student there.
Was your Copland experience during that year; was it at Julliard?
Was that before or after?
It may have been in between leaving college and going to Julliard; I'm not sure, or it may have been right after Julliard. No, no, it was before Julliard.
I went from Julliard--I went from college to Copland to Julliard and back to college but in the post grad music courses.
We managed to skip over the college experience. What school was it?
N.Y.U.
This is while I was still a pre-med student.
Were you a good pre-med student?
No, very bad.
I was asked to leave college, I was asked to leave Julliard. I asked myself to leave Copland, I was asked to leave N.Y.U. when I went back there as a music student. As a student I was bad.
What brought you back? By this time you should catch onto your own pattern, why did you come back?
To Julliard?
No, to N.Y.U.?
I knew that I wanted to continue in music, I was just reaching out in all directions, trying to find a place that would fit, that would feel right, and so I kept looking. But nothing felt right.
How did you meet Copland?
Through my mother. She found him for me.
Did he have a number of students in those days?
He was teaching. I
He was not then the great man that he is now?

He was known to be a great composer in those days, but I don't think he was very secure financially. Of course I only judge by where he was living, where he was teaching, the kind of surroundings he had. Even that was not a good experience. He didn't give me anything but opinions.
Do you remember the first day you confronted him, the day you met him and talked about why you were there? Do you recall any of those conversations?

No, I don't. I was pretty much still being guided by my family, by my mother and father. With all my resentments, fightings against, I still didn't realize that I could guide myself if I wanted to, or that's all I had left, to go searching my own way.
In those days I was still being controlled and accepting it.
Did you have hope each time that it was going to be different?
With Copland?
With Copland or any of them; did you think this was going to be a good experience?
I always had those hopes but as you said, I began to recognize a pattern that perhaps going to an individual or to an institution to be taught those things wasn't the way.
How did you work with him, or how did he work with you?

He would ask me to write melodies; that's all he ever asked me to do during the period of time I was with him, and I would play them to him, I think the first week that I went to him I may have worked everyday trying to write stuff for him, then I came in and he liked this and he didn't like that and why didn't I

take this and develop it up a little higher and bring it higher and I said because I felt that it was going lower and lower. I couldn't appreciate this kind of-- that wasn't teaching, he wasn't telling me anything. He was telling me his likes and dislikes.
He never told you anything--
About me. He was telling me about Aaron Copland.

So I got so that I would do my work for him on the train ride up to his studio. I wouldn't work at all all week, I played ball and on the day of the lesson I'd get on the train, take out the manuscript paper and the pencil and write fifty melodies on the way up.
He liked some of those melodies, presumably?
He liked some of them.
Was that the way he worked, that was his teaching method?
I couldn't really believe--I think he didn't take me seriously and I didn't take him seriously at all.
Did your paths ever cross in later years?

I attended a concert that he gave at the Brooklyn Museum, the museum on Eastern Parkway. He gave a concert there and I went up to him after the concert and said hello. He remembered me and smiled and shook my hand.
Did he remember your work other than--
My melodies?
Did he remember you as a student, as a teenager, or later?
He remembered as the young teenager.
He didn't know what you had done otherwise?
This wasn't this many years later.
You hadn't become
rich and famous and able to go back to your old professor?
I haven't become that yet. Happy I've become, but rich and famous, no.
You still have time to go back to Copland and say now, here we are.
Yeah; not very much time though. A little bit.

I did enjoy his work though; I must say that. As a teacher--actually I don't know if he was serious in the way he was teaching me. Maybe I was just part of his income, that's all he could see when he looked at me.
You've taught kids yourself, subsequently.
Right, and you can tell from kids. Yeah, he may have gotten bad vibes from me, but I did go to him originally with hope.
Was he expensive? Was it a sacrifice?
I didn't handle it, so
I really didn't know. I don't think he was cheap. In those days my father was making good money, and he probably knew it.
Did he ask you to leave or did you?
No, I gave it up. I announced to the family one day I didn't want to continue anymore.
Did he ever work with you as a player at all or this was all strictly composition?
It was all composition.
You have a reputation as something of a ball player too and you keep referring to going and playing ball then. Over your later professional life, you were big on softball if I remember correctly.
I was big on a lot of sports. I loved to play ball. But we grow old. Who was that guy--
(Unintelligible)
You played football?
We were kids then, dear. That was Allie Sherman, he became the coach of the New
York Giants.
You grew up together over in Brooklyn?
He was my kid brother's friend, he lived in the same building that we did.
And you taught him to play football?
I didn't teach him to play football.
I like that better; that could be a headline on the tape.
I used to practice with him during the day. Yeah, I could have taught him I guess; sounds good though.
He's not going to come back and argue about it.
I don't know.
After leaving Copland, at that point you must have decided what you were going to do.
Right. I was still being poked by my family not to be a bum, to do
nothing, so then I tried Julliard but nothing happened there and then I went back--when I went to N.Y.U. originally for pre-med that was the uptown place; that's become Bronx Community College today.
When I went back I went to the downtown school, which is the only N.Y.U. that's left.
I think so.
That's where I went and took a few courses there.

I studied composition there with Marion Bauer. She was a pretty decent composer herself, but once again, I like this, I don't like that; why didn't you go up there instead of down and it doesn't reach me, an approach like that. I don't want people's opinions.
These were, I assume, friendly conversations?
Right. She was a very nice person.
At this point, this
This is about '38.
(Side A of Tape 1 ended at this point. Transcript will continue with Side B.)
You were about twenty years old?
Yes.
And ready to strike out?
I was twenty in 1940. Right, it was about '38 at this time.
While I was downstairs, the Benny Goodman Trio, Gene Krupa and Benny and Teddy Wilson were very big, and Krupa came down to N.Y.U. to give a jazz concert.

He came down alone so they searched through the school to find a clarinet player and a piano player and they found me and another guy and we played the thing with Gene. I remember calling him a few years after that, when he formed
his own band; he didn't remember me. I never got to join his band.
What did they ask you to do to get a clarinet player and a piano player, to do the Benny Goodman charts?

He came down and said let's do one chorus of "Idaho", then give me two stop choruses and clarinet take one and then we'll all go out with one, and he named a few tunes to try and find out what we knew. I didn't know the clarinet player and he didn't know me, we had no idea, but we put it together and it was a fun day.
That was your first brush with the big time?
Right. That was it.
Krupa was not very old then either, was he? I've forgotten his age. He's older than you but not a hell of a lot.
No, probably by about six, seven years.
He was about twenty-
No, I think he was about ten years older than me. He's gone now, isn't he? Of course Gene's gone.
He's gone ten years or more.
I keep forgetting how many guys are gone. They kept dropping year by year.
He worked hard on dropping year by year.
A lot of us did. I'm really astonished that I still haven't. I never would have believed in my early days that I would have gone passed thirty.
We'll get into that later on.
I'm not really getting into anything.
I want to ask about some of that later on. Was there any response in you to
play in this gig with Krupa? Did you say now it's time for me to go out and get on that level?

It charged me up a great deal. I wanted to, but it was too tough to break in. I was still a little too young, I wasn't all that great as a jazz pianist. I never thought I'd been all that great as a jazz pianist.
How did you play then? Can you characterize it? Did you play like everybody else then or was it a recognizable--how would you characterize it?
Below average jazz playing.
Not in chops, obviously. You've always had pretty good chops if I recall.

My chops are fairly good, but I have to remind you that what I call my bullshitting I can make it sound like they're great chops but it's not really happening. I don't know how to call this ability I have of doing that, but it's not really the legitimate
article. It's not the note for note perfection that's required.
Were you playing what in those days was traditional piano, the moving left hand and that sort of thing?
Yes, the oompa, oompa.
Who were you listening to, what piano players were you listening to then?
Teddy Wilson and Jess Stacy; some of the guys that were around then, Fats Waller. Then I heard Tatum, he was something, he was tremendous.
Were you aware of Ellington's work at that time, more than casually aware of?
I wasn't as aware of it as I had become later on. I got to the people I felt I should have listened to earlier--I got to them later. But thank God I got to them.
Were you listening to particular writers in those days?

I was listening to bands in those days. I wasn't really too together in understanding what was happening with the bands, I never thought who was writing the stuff. I guess I just assumed that it grew on the stands. Each leader had his own seeds and the damn music grew.

One of the things I remember--I was always fascinated that DownBeat-- that Stan Kenton would be the favorite band and Sy Oliver was always the favorite arranger; having nothing to do with each other of course.
Sy Oliver was a name that everybody remembered, so he always got the vote.
A lot of his things were popular, they were big record sellers. He was a popular writer.
Did you think in those days of being more than instrumental, were you thinking of writing for a band?
Yes. I recognized right away that I'd rather write than play, and that's

what I did as I developed myself; I played less and wrote more. Not even when I finished with Boyd-- when I was about halfway through the Boyd Raeburn experience, I stopped playing, I was just writing. (Marmarosa) I think that's when Dodo joined the band.
What was your first for pay arrangement, the first real businesslike chart you ever wrote?
There was a bandleader, a real nutty guy who became a magician, he was well known, I can't think of his name right now--
Richard Himber.
Richard Himber; right. A red headed, stocky kind of guy.
He had a big magic act as part of his act.
He wasn't tall though, he was wide. Yeah. I heard that he was looking for charts and he was rehearsing in some studio and I went up to see him and he gave me a list of

tunes that he wanted in his book. He said pick one out and do a chart on it. I picked on out, did a chart on it. I don't remember what it was at all, but that was it, that was the first time I got paid for a job. I brought it in and he liked it.
Did you follow up and write more?
I think I wrote one other thing for him.
Do you remember the first time you heard it played?
At the rehearsal.
Do you remember your reaction the first time a real professional band played your piece of music?
I was very pleased. It's always great to hear your music.
Did you rehearse the band and do the whole nine yards, as they say, on the Navy band?
No, they did it; I was

a spectator. I just put the music on the stands and whoever was rehearsing the band--I don't think it was Himber, I think he had another guy there rehearsing the band for him, probably his number one arranger. He just ran it down, there was nothing involved, there were no time changes or anything, you just tap the thing off and it starts and ends by itself.
I sat there and made a few mental notes like, my God, why did I do that, and gee, that sounds pretty good. I learned by listening. This was a good idea and that wasn't a good idea.
How much did they pay for charts then; do you remember?

I remember that it was unbelievably low. He probably paid me one-tenth of what he paid the other people because I was a new kid, I was inexperienced, I didn't know what the prices were. He could have given me $15 for the chart.
Didn't a lot of people work for that kind of money anyway in those days?
I don't think you could get a chart for less than fifty bucks in those days.
I remember the first time I--actually my first big name band--you know, when you're a young musician, the pinnacle of what you could become is to be in a name band; it's nothing beyond that, right?
True.
That's the top of the world, if you're in a name band you've reached it.

So at the age of twenty, 1940, I joined the Raymond Scott band. He was auditioning pianists and I took my shot. I had gone with a bunch of other guys; he liked my touch and he picked me. I think he picked me for a few reasons, my touch and the fact that I was a young kid and he could probably save a lot of money on me.
Did he know your work otherwise, your writing?
No. He had no idea that I could write.

There's some irony I guess to the fact that you worked with him, because the two of you had the same kind of humor and surprise later on in your work. It wasn't the same kind of music at all, but the same element of surprise land mines around.
Raymond was a very weird guy and most people disliked him. I didn't dislike him, I got along with him perfectly.
Let me switch something here.

He was the guy who had gotten all those inventive little things that he had written for his quintet, and it wasn't that I enjoyed these pieces of his musically, I just enjoyed the fact that they were different, that he had the courage to be different, to write just the way he felt. That's what knocked me out about him.
Did he write all that
Yes.
The stuff he's known for.
"Twilight in Turkey"?
Yes.
"Wild Night on an Ocean"
Yes.

Yeah, those are his. I joined his quintet and then it became a big band and we went on tour. He had a manager named Harvey Bacall who really took advantage of me. One night he found out that I could write--they were having me write for them-- as we toured around, we'd get into town and Raymond would say to me I need a chart on "My Mama Done Told Me" for Dorothy and I want to do it in the show this afternoon. He'd tell me that in the morning. So I'd get in my hotel room and write the chart for him and Dorothy would sing it.
Which Dorothy?
Dorothy Collins. She was fifteen years old at the time, travelling with her mother and singing with the band.
He married her later on.
She later on was on the Hit Parade. As a matter of fact, his brother was the Hit Parade band Mark Warnow.
He took it over when Mark died.
Did he?
Right.
But then at the end of the week at salary time, I would find ten dollars added to my salary for the charts. That was really offensive to me.
Were you copying it too?
Yes. I really was deeply hurt by that. Then I went to Ray and I said Raymond this is not nice of you people to do this

to me, how can you actually think that you can pay a man ten dollars for all this work. He didn't want to know about it. Harvey handles that, and talk to Harvey. I couldn't handle these fast talking people; I have trouble enough today handling a fast talker, except that I have no problem recognizing them anymore.
That's half the battle.

Yeah. Those people have dug holes in my life with their fast talking. However, that's what finally caused the separation between Raymond and myself. Harvey Bacall, his manager, decided that he could write music too so he started to write little charts, and my God, they were terrible.
Were any of your things recorded?
By Raymond?
Yes.
I don't know. No, not actually on record, but I've had some--I don't
have them anymore; I may have them but I don't know where they are. I used to keep air checks of the stuff I wrote for him, I'd take it off the air, hold onto them.
He used to do my stuff in theaters, after I left him I'd go watch the band in a show, in a theater and he was using my stuff.
At this point, if you ever find them, it would be worthwhile to have them to add to this document we're creating here.
How could they be useful? You mean the stuff that I wrote for Raymond?
Yes, sure; it's part of you in any case.
The only value it would have is historical.
That's what I'm talking about.
Anything about me is valuable historically.
That's why we're here.
Oh, I keep forgetting.
You have now become famous, if not rich.
This is our secret though.
Is it fair to say that there's a similarity between your--this is hardly musical, but your title and Raymond's titles are not dissimilar.

I wasn't affected by his titles. His titles didn't give me an idea for my titles. My titles came with the music; sometimes before the music I would fantasize something or see something. If it was a title it also had a picture or a story in my head, and I would almost tailor-make the music as if I was accompanying a movie or something, because the movie was going on in my mind. Most of the things I wrote were programmatic, and the titles weren't just titles, they were stories. I'm sure that I picked out titles just for the hell of it.
Your music has always
been essentially humorous, as the titles.
Humorous and angry. I could recognize all the anger in my music and it's full of anger.
But it's also full of the release of the humor and the inside jokes and such.
Of course you heard it, I sent you the tape of that "Bloos" thing that I had written for the Norman Granz album.
Yes.

On the original score-- I don't know how well you examine the score, but if you did, you'd notice the certain section on the drummer's part, there's a spot where I want him to blow a razzer; did you see that?
No.

The band--I don't know, it was actually in a dramatic part of the music, I was discussing blues, all the things that blues could be and I got into something deep, momentarily deep and suddenly from out of that came the

cliche blues phrases, that everybody and his uncle is using which was like a momentary aside. I went into a cliche phrase, da-da-da-da. I put it in the trumpets and I think I put it in the bones and I put it the flute ba-ba-ba.
Yes, I recall.

And then the hell with it, razzer, and then we continue with the music. And that was a part of it, part of the thought and part of the music, considering the fact that it was a musical aside; the hell with this cliche crap, let's get back to reality. This is what it was in the music.

Barry Ulanov, who is associated with Metronome at the time, was at the recording and Barry came flying out of the studio, the control room, 'Stop!' I said, 'what's the matter?' He said, 'you can't do that!' I said, 'of course I can do it! Not only can I do it, I just did it; what do you mean, I can't do it!' He said, 'you can not do that, that's Dadaism!' I didn't know what the hell he meant, what's Dadaism?
I know what Dadaism is. I don't know what he means.
I found out. You can't use the real article to depict music.
It's a fine point but I guess I do understand what he was saying.
That's what he was saying.
If you could do it with a trumpet it would be valid.
Right.

I said Barry, I understand what you're saying, but I don't agree with you. Of course I can use the razzer, that's exactly the sound I want, and what else could infer the inference that I want to make. 'You can't do it.' I didn't want to argue so I said all right. I had a contrabassoon there, so I said take it off the drums and contrabassoon, play your lowest note at that time. So I got my razzer out of the contrabassoon.
It lives today at the
end of each Muppet Show. What lives? Exactly the same expression. Did you ever watch the Muppet Show sometimes on Saturday afternoon?
No.

It ends with a little piece of music, a little jazz thing, and it ends with a basic bop-bop, and a tenor blowing a low vulgar B flat solo note. It's exactly the same statement, done by one of the muppets whose name is Zoot, as a matter of fact.
That's fantastic. Today it's all right.
I'm not sure-- granting that there is such a thing as Dadaism, I'm not sure why he would choose to say you can't be a da-da.
I didn't think it was important to stop the recording to get into it, whatever it was.
Barry was a nice guy, I liked him, I didn't want to get into anything with him.
Was he there as sort of a consultant to Norman?
He was a visitor. He had no right to stop anything, but we were all friends. It was all right.
Norman was willing to pay the extra money for the extra time Barry was costing him.
Imagine a visitor running out of a control booth today in a recording session.
It wouldn't happen. As a matter of fact today I don't think Barry would run out of the studio.
No, probably not. At that point you had worked for Himber; if I remember that was a tenor band, wasn't it? It had a violin section?
There were no strings in this band that he had.
But it was a hotel
It was a hotel band. I'm sure you're right, it was a tenor band.
And Ray Scott was a hundred and eighty degrees off of that.
Right.
And anything than traditional.
Right.
You had had a vast spectrum there in the very early days. Where did you go then after Scott?
I don't remember the order of things, but there were trips with various bands. I mentioned the name to you last night, Michael Loring; he wasn't one of the most popular bands in the country.
Was he a hotel band? As they refer to now, a sweet band?
A society band? No, he was a full grown, six brass, four saxes, he carried a girl trio, singing trio, boy singer,

himself fronting and he was a singer. So he was a large hotel band and they played popular music of the day. It wasn't a jazz band, it wasn't a sweet band, it was just your average big band of the day.
Like a Bob Chester kind?
Right. I went from him to Bob Chester to Muggsy Spanier.

Talk about Bob Chester a minute. He's always intrigued me, perhaps because it's through an awful lot of mist I look back at it, I recall that as a hell of a good band and one of the great themes of all times was his theme, and now that I mentioned that, I'd love to think you wrote it.
His theme?
'Starburst.'
I don't remember his theme.
Ba-da-ba-da--your
typical big band theme. I guess you didn't write it; I would have liked to think you did.
I didn't remember it.
I'll play it for you after a while.
Really?
A great theme. He was from a wealthy family as I recall.

Right. Ford Motor Company or one of those. He was from Detroit I know. He had automobile money behind him. Bob didn't live like a very rich man; I don't think he had his family's money while he was a band leader. He may have done that against the family wishes; maybe they chopped him off. I really don't know, but he was a nice guy, he was a very decent sort of person, easy going, gave nobody problems.
It was kind of a Glenn Miller band, wasn't it?
Similar.
He wasn't as thorough a perfectionist as Miller was. As a matter of fact, Bob didn't care that much, he was very easy going.
Were you playing on the band too?
I was playing with the band. I wrote a few things probably; I don't remember. I usually write something for every band I've ever been with.

Then I joined--where was this--this was right after I came out of the army, that was '41, '42, probably just the band before Raeburn, I joined Jack Teagarden; I stayed with him for about a year, toured the South, had a ball with him. There was a player, I loved to hear him play.

One of the big thrills of my life was the beginning of every night working with Jack Teagarden, just to hear him pick up the horn and play his theme, 'I've Got a Right to Sing the Blues'. It's hard to describe, I just got such a warm feeling when he would start that.
That set the night for me.
I heard he was a very personal player, everything he did was very personal.
Talk about your relationship with him, what kind of a guy he was.

Jack was as easy going a person as I've ever come across. He probably could handle anything that happened, nothing seemed to phase him. He was amused by me, he used to call me the Professor, because when I would write for him, he would hear harmonies that he never heard before, sounds that he didn't think could come out of bands, so he called me the Professor.

I did a chart on "Body and Soul" for him that I wish I had today; I really worked on it, worked very hard, one of the few times I worked hard to accomplish something and it must have been very involved because he gave me that questioning look at times, that amused look, the Professor's at it again, but he was an amazing
man. I really loved him.
Did he like your work or was he being tolerant and amused?
No, he liked it. I could tell; he didn't have to tell me anything.
Do you supposed that piece music exists on air check someplace, 'Body and Soul?'
I don't know.
We may be able to find it somewhere.
I really don't know.
Jack Tower has--not Jack, Jerry Valburn has a house full of air checks.
(Side B of Tape 1 ended at this point. Transcript will continue in accordance with Tape 2.)
Of Teagarden?
I don't know for sure if he's got Teagarden, but I'll search around for it.
I don't recall us ever doing it on the air.
If it was done somewhere, somebody's got it.

We weren't on the air too much. I can't recall--once I think we did an army base and I think that was broadcast, but I don't think it was ever put on the air. I just happened to think of something I haven't thought of in years. Jack, by reputation and in fact was a drinker, this man could consume cases and still walk straight, and he was married at the time--her name was Addie and she was managing the band and she was an aviatix too; she was quite a woman. She drank, she matched him bottle for bottle and we were in Mobile once playing a theater and during the morning I heard a commotion out in the hall, and I opened my door and looked out and I saw a bunch of cops dragging Jack out of his room and he was covered with blood, pouring down his head, and they dragged Addie out too; she was

covered with blood. What had happened was that they were drinking in their room, drinking and drinking and arguing and the arguing got into an all-out brawl and Addie broke a whiskey bottle across Jack's chops, right across his mouth. We didn't know how the hell--of course he wasn't going to show up for the show, they certainly were going to keep him in the hospital overnight at least. So we were talking about what to do, what to do and word came down, don't worry, just go straight ahead. So we were in the pit and suddenly Jack walked in, took his place and the stage came up and he was covered with bandages. He had just had a whiskey bottle broken over his face, picked up his horn and went boo-boo-boo-da-da-da, just as perfect as ever. He played the whole thing after that. I never forgot that. I thought that was one of the wildest things I'd ever seen.
Was he injured at all or just lucky?
I have no idea. I was
He was a big tough guy.
You talk about the stoic Indian?
He was from Texas, wasn't he? Waco, Texas if I remember.
Yes, he was from Texas; right.

He's quoted as saying something not unlike you, somebody was talking about what he did, the technique that went into his work and the thought that went into his playing, and the emotions that went into his playing and as an aside he said, that's all horseshit, I just play what I can think of.
You do what you have to and you hope that you're doing it in a way that will reach what you think you're trying to reach. That's one point, and then of course the other

point is if you're reproducing something that's been written and you've got to get every note out perfectly, and if you can make people believe that you're doing that, you're accomplishing something, even if you're not actually producing what they think you're producing.
From the other side, were you or are you tough on players who don't reproduce exactly what you've asked them to?

I'm not a tough guy, in any sense. I'm tough on nobody. If people don't reproduce what I ask them to, and they're not capable of doing it, well I discover that and I make a decision; do I want them anyway, should I adjust to them or am I insistent on what I want? If I am insistent in having what I want, I would have to change the man. But otherwise--

When you were doing (Sally)" the thing for Boyd, "Dalvatore" and "k.y F" and all that material which was astonishing to those people I'm sure, and puzzling, were you satisfied with what they finally did in performance?
Yeah; right. You better switch that off for a moment.

I found out that the last bit of this thing, I didn't have the tape running properly, I had to go over twenty, thirty minutes of the interview again which didn't make him very happy at all. He didn't understand why I was there anyway. He had a major part of the world to run that morning. We skipped over your stint in the army; how do we fit that in?
Let me see. 1941--it was December, 1941. 1942, I was drafted in about September. I was in about-- did we ever discover how long I was in the army, Babe?
About six or eight months.
It wasn't even a full year. I spent my time in the army down
in Oklahoma, in Muskogee with the Rainbow Division and that's where I left the army from Camp what?
Fort Ord?
No.
Sill?
No.
Those are the only two Oklahoma camps I remember.
No, this is--Camp Gruber, in Muskogee, Oklahoma.

I was discharged from there, came back in time to run into a guy who I had associated myself with just before I went to the army, a saxophone player named Herbie Fields. I had once told Herbie that if he ever wanted to be a band leader, I'd be happy to write a book for him. I thought he should be a band leader, I felt he had the ability to front a band.
I was still in uniform and I ran into Herbie and he had a guy with him that was going to be his manager--Pete something, who

became Monty Kay's partner--Pete Cameron. We got together and we decided to create a band for Herbie to front. I spent some time with that, we developed a book and we auditioned for a few hotels; we never quite got going, but we had a pretty good little band after a while.
Why did it not get going? Was it lack of money?
I don't know. I really don't know. That was actually the beginning of my own personal involvement in getting a band off the ground.
Tell me, when you decided to write a book for Herbie Fields, did you consciously say this was going to have this kind of "sound" and you built the book architecturally?
No. I had no idea of a particular sound.
By that I mean like the Miller, clarinet thing.
I understand. No, I

didn't have a sound in mind or style. I probably felt that you did the best you could with each individual piece of material and try to present it the best way you can. That's a pretty good style of its own.

With that premise in mind, we got it together. It was a heck of a good band and a good book. As a matter of fact, when the band disintegrated and Herbie joined Lionel Hampton he took some of those charts with him and would use them with his band, to feature Herbie.

I remember running into them in Boston a few years later and Herbie said "this is Hamp, George Handy, this is the guy that wrote the "Body and Soul" that we do, the "Stardust" that we do," and he said, "oh yeah, I got to have you write for my band." "I'd be happy to, man. Okay."
The guy that was managing him, Hampton, is one of the big agents--I can't think of his name--
Willard Alexander?
It wasn't him; it was
another one. It was a hard nose guy in terms of business, spoke like a gangster.
Ben Pollock.
Ben Pollock? No, no, no.
What about Bullets?
No, it wasn't Bullets.

I'll probably think of the name.
He was a well known, bigoted guy.
Anyway, he came into the room and Hamp said, I want you to meet George Handy, he's the guy that wrote those charts that we're so happy with and the guy said, terrific and Lionel said I want him to do about four or five things and the guy said yeah, great. He said, incidentally, what do you charge? I said well, the fact that we have a package here of four to five things, let me give you a decent price, say a hundred a chart, which was cheap, even in those days.
This guy said, forget it, a hundred a chart, are you kidding? I can get the greatest writers in the world for a hundred dollars a chart. I said well, get them; I'm not writing for less than

that and that ended my writing for Hampton. I remember still being astonished of the fact that band leaders couldn't make their own decisions. I guess I wasn't willing to accept the fact that a band leader doesn't have control of his band.
They generally didn't have control of the money, presumably then.
That's where all the power was. That was that experience. I can always say I almost wrote for Lionel Hampton. It was a name like Willard Alexander. It wasn't Willard.
It will pop up. Was that your experience with managers all through your career, presumably?

Generally I think it was. I didn't have that much contact with managers. I think, for the most part, that I could make the deal with the band leader himself, and that whoever the money was would accept his
judgement; whatever deal he made they would back him up.
At this point you considered yourself an arranger?
Right.
And that was your career?
Right. I knew that I was more than an arranger; I knew that I was a composer.
I meant as opposed to player.

Oh. Yeah. I always felt there was something missing in my musical makeup in terms of jazz, and that was the ease of sitting inside a swinging time, and being able to sit there at ease and play. I recognized that I would tighten up when I tried to play a jazz solo and get into a lot of cliche crap rather than being what I would do when I would write, pure inventive. I would get hung--you found it.
Is it fair to say-- if I recall, now that you mentioned it, on the jazz things that you wrote for yourself, like "Foolish Little Boy"--you were on the band then, weren't you?
Yes.
And some of the other things that you wrote--
That was written for Dodo though--"Foolish Little Boy". I wrote it in his honor.
You anticipated Dodo's foolishness, I guess.
He was kind of foolish then.
In any case, the things that you wrote for yourself, you did not use extended jazz solos, but conversations with the band back and forth, sort of, if I recall that material.
Probably.
Were you conscious
of doing it that way?

I was aware that I couldn't write music featuring myself as a jazz pianist, because I never felt that my jazz playing was on a worthwhile level, having people listening to me, as being a great inventive jazz player.

There are times when I play where I have that good feel and I'll play pretty decent, enough to satisfy me, so as far as I'm concerned, that's the only criteria, if I'm pleased with what I'm doing, I don't care what other people think. I have to satisfy me.

So I avoid writing for me as a soloist, the same way I would avoid writing for anyone else in the band that didn't play good jazz. I would give him another role, other than soloist. I'd do the same thing for me, as a jazz player.
Now, that is, as opposed to other situations, where I may want an involved piano passage which would require a hell of a good
pianist to play it, but this I would write for myself, because I could train myself to play any passage.
I've explained that--that I bullshit--that's my term, I bullshit. I don't really do the precise thing. I do it a shade away but I, most of the time, would defy anybody to tell me the difference.
You've made some records as pianist on quartet or a trio. It seemed to me I found some over there this morning.

I don't turn down jobs or income, so if anybody wants to hire me to make a record with a bunch of jazz players, of course I'll do it. I comp well, I know that. I know that I can back up a soloist adequately and good jazz players have told me they love to play with me backing them up. But when it comes to me doing the solo work, I get hung; it's when I suddenly get into an area which I realize I'm not that competent in.
And it's the same now
as it was many years ago.
It affects my damn playing of the moment and just interferes with it.
You've never been able to ease that or get accustomed to it?
There have been times when I forget that I stink, and I play well.

As a little aside, I did a piece for the magazine on hypnosis as an aide to playing, and that was very much what the hypnotist said, you have to convince yourself that you don't stink and then you will play well.
I'm sure of that.
Granting a certain amount of basic ability, all the rest of it is all overcoming your own self imposed problems.
I would have loved to have taken the hypnotic route, but I've never been able to be hypnotized. I cannot get myself in a receptive frame of mind to allow someone
Have you tried to be hypnotized?

During my early years of personal problems, I've gone the route of hypnotherapy, I've gone to supposedly very excellent doctors. I was with Dr. Walberg who was the pioneer of hypnotherapy. He wrote the definitive books on it too. After a number of sessions I would constantly tell him the same thing, you didn't hypnotize me, I wasn't under, and he would say you wouldn't know. How could he say I wouldn't know when I did know and I know now, I wasn't hypnotized. Well, you were in the stage that was satisfactory.
At any rate, there was no long term effect of the hypnosis?
I wasn't hypnotized. He did not have me in a hypnotic--
I'll report on the progress of this for the second part of the story,
the next issue I'm going to be hypnotized over the telephone and we'll see if it improves my playing.

My theory was, and he agreed, whether he accepts--with hypnosis you can improve your concentration and make for much smoother execution of things, simply by paying more attention to them. He said it's worth a try.
I would think so. I absolutely would think so.
Have you been hypnotized?
No, never.
You never even tried?
I've never seen a hypnotist except in stage shows where they put a girl between two chairs and stand on her and that kind of garbage, which is not what this is at all.
He thinks that kind of show of hypnosis gives the science a bad name, which I'm sure he would like to think of himself as a therapist instead of a showman.
I'll let you know how it works. If I play any better, I'll bottle it and sell it.
Who is this guy?

His name is--I can't tell you--he's in St. Paul, Minnesota, he's worked with Rod Carew. I learned about it on a sport show. He worked with Carew on concentration which is very important in baseball, it's one of the principles.
I remember Carew saying that his work with the man--
It's Harvey Maizel. He also worked with the Minnesota Symphony.
The entire orchestra?
No, with some of the individuals.

He works on referrals from doctors; it's sort of an early stage therapy kind of practice, I gather, but anyway, we'll see if it works. I consider it terribly valid; it may not help me but as a theory, I think from our
conversations, it seems to be entirely valid. Why not? We know that we're limited by our own hangups, so if you can wipe some of that aside, then it seems simple.
Right.
What did you do in the army?
I was made a litter bearer--what am I talking about--is that what they call it when you carry the stretcher?
Yeah. It is a litter.
That's what I was.
In MASH, they say litter bearers.

That's what I was, I was a litter bearer. I didn't want to bear lit- ters, it didn't appeal to me and I applied for a transfer to the band. I went to see my command- ing officer and I told him I didn't feel happy here, I wanted to transfer to the band and he said he didn't have much hope for it, but he put

the request in.
I went down and met some of the guys in the band and hung out for a little while with them and played with some of them, then I forgot about it and I got used to my group and I started to like the guys that I was bearing litters with and one day, the commanding officer sent for me and I went in to see him and he said, your transfer came through, you can go join the band, and I asked him if it was possible for me to forget about the transfer and stay where I was and he asked me why and I told him, well, I got used to what I'm doing, I like the people I'm working with, I'm comfortable, I'd like to stay. Of course he dug that and anyway they didn't transfer me. I stayed where I was.
Then I got this spur on my heel and couldn't walk; that ended my army career. I did very little except be homesick.
What kind of a band was this? This was a dance band, I gather?
They played dance--it
was the army band.
You would have been the cymbal player or something in the marching band?
Tuba.
You played tuba?

No, but I grabbed the horn and managed to conquer an octave, then I felt I didn't need any more than an octave in order to get along. I didn't need the damn music either, my ears could tell me where it was going; so I was a tuba player. It was funny as hell. Not then, but now that I think about it.
Did you audition on the tuba? Did you have an honest to God audition like they do now in the service bands?

Do they? No, I didn't have to. They wanted me for the other band for playing piano in the dance band, but of course it was my choice of what instrument. They were perfectly satisfied to have me fake it or not play at all, just make believe I was playing.
Was there anybody else on the band that you ran into later?
I didn't get to know any of those guys well, any of the musicians. I wasn't there that long. I spent most of the time with my outfit, not the musicians.

I'm curious, your life had been--up to that moment--nothing but music and your associations were nothing but musicians and you had, I would assume, very little in common with the litter bearers, do you see what I'm getting at?
Yeah.
Why you didn't want to rush back into your own milieu.

This is 1942 and I'm twenty two years old. I came back to music when I was about fifteen, I guess and for a few years it was nothing but kids and kid bands and learning and listening, so I wasn't really that full of music and musical friends and musical life. As a matter of fact, there was very little of it

up to that point. I had made some contacts, some friends, I had done a little musical work, but I wasn't that full of it so that I could have said my life up to that point had been nothing but music. I spent more time I guess up to then, playing ball than I did anything else. That was my love.
Did you ever think that you might become a professional ballplayer?
Yes. I had to make a decision whether to go out for sports or go out for music.
Were you a better ballplayer?
I think so. I think I would have done probably best in football, although I was a good baseball player. I was probably championship caliber in swimmer--I was a speed swimmer. That's it.
