If circumstances had brushed you against a scout for the Cardinals or for the New York Giants, would you have been perfectly happy to have been plucked out of this and become a ball player?

Well, I don't know, it would have depended on what was offered to me and whether it would have affected me. If they had offered what I thought would have been a lot of money, I might have done it, because at that time of my life there were three things that gave me pleasure, music, sports and sex.
You can't make much money in sex, so that would be--
No. You could but not me. I was not the gigolo, whoreish type.

What did you do with the litter bearer, did your music find any expression at all? Were they interested in your experience as a young player? Did you talk about it or was it an almost musicless period?
Right. There was

nobody that I could relate to in the music area; I never got close to anybody, because away from the place where we played, I was away from it totally and I could only manage to get down there maybe one or two days a week and for perhaps an hour at a time, so I never got close to the guys in the band and I didn't play much with them, just a few occasions. The fact that they wanted me was important; I guess that's what kept bringing me back.
But I did recognize the fact that I didn't want to leave my outfit to join the band. I think originally I was probably afraid to be a litter bearer.
That gets right into the thick of the action.
You better believe it. The thought of it scared the hell out of me. Well, I don't think I was any different than anybody else, everybody in the army was scared stiff.
I guess that was in no way an expression of your medical background.

I've often wondered why they took me for that, because I didn't pick-- when you're offered three choices I didn't opt for the band--any of the choices. I think number one I wanted the Air Force, number two I think I wanted tanks and not music.
Did you fly then?
No. I had flown commercially.
But you didn't own a private airplane?
No. I don't know why the hell I picked it that way either. I might have had a reason then.
Sometimes those reasons get lost very quickly.
Right.
We can get into some of the bands you worked with after the Army, with Himber and Chester, and who else were you mentioning?
Teagarden
Was that Teagarden's big band or was that one of the eight or nine piece?
No, it was a big band. Three trumpets, three trombones, with him it made four, five saxes.
Do you recall who some of the players were?
I remember two of the trumpet players. One guys name was Snuffy Claus. His brother Charlie, had been with the band just before I joined.
He was a trumpet player, wasn't he?
Right. Charlie left the band the day before I joined up.
There was a little guy that played the jazz solos, a little, tiny man, skinny and most fragile human you would ever want to see and he played beautifully, but this guy--I don't think
I ever saw him sober, he was out of it every moment of the day. His name was Stirling Bowes-- did you ever hear that name?
I don't think so.
Stirling Bowes.
A trumpet jazz player?
He was a Dixieland type player, but so beautifully; oh, he played so beautiful. He was such a pain in the ass otherwise.

We were once on the road driving and I was in the car with Stirling, Jack was--no, Adie was driving and Jack was sitting next to her and Stirling and I were in the back seat and Stirling kept cursing in his drunken stupor and Jack was saying, 'come on, Jack, calm down, there's a woman in the car, have a little respect.' 'Fuck you and fuck her and fuck this and fuck that.' So Jack said, 'Stirling,--now we're on a stretch of road in the South and you can't see anything in front or anything in back, nothing--and Jack said 'if you don't stop that Stirling, I'm going to put

you out of the car." "I don't give a fuck, fuck you, fuck her," and they stopped the car and Jack pulled him out of the car and threw him on the road and they drove off and left him there. I couldn't believe it, and he appeared a couple of days later on the gig. I have no idea how he got there.
He didn't go back after him?
No, he left him there. He left him there and drove hundreds of more miles to the next gig.
I said, "Jack, how can you do that," and he said, "I don't give a god damn; that's as much as I can take from him."
When he showed up he had bruises, he was black and blue and filthy.
Did he drink any less?
No. He never changed, Stirling. He continued the same way.
You had to love the guy because he was so fragile and such a sweet man, a lovely man,
but he was impossible when he got drunk. He couldn't play beyond a certain point of drinking, he couldn't even get a sound out of his instrument.
In those days--we're talking really about 1942 and '43, in those days, I gather that the recreation on the band was drinking as opposed to dope.

Right. That's when I started drinking, when I joined the Teagarden band--no, it wasn't when I joined the Teagarden band, it was when I joined the Raymond Scott band. Everybody pulled their own bottle under their coats; I had never seen this before, every guy in the band with his own quart of whiskey, my god, so I went out and bought mine and I started to drink with everybody else.
The miraculous thing is, looking back, is that some of these guys were such good drinkers
What do you mean by good drinkers?
They were able to at least perform after drinking predigious amounts of booze.
Right; fantastic. But past a certain point--I don't know how they could tell what that point was--some of them knew just how far they could take it, which is what you're saying.
Yeah.
But guys like Stirling they took it passed the point of being able to perform.
How did the managers react to this, were they all the time running around yelling and screaming to stop it? They were, after all, responsible to the money.
Jack's manager was his wife and she drank as much as he did.
That was also part of Jack's trademark, I guess, his drinking.
I think so too.
Part of the act.

I would say to describe my musical life before joining Boyd that it was one in which I had been told that I was going to be in medicine, I was going to become a doctor, which I didn't doubt, I just accepted blindly and one of feeling musical stirrings in me, recognizing that I had an appetite for music, but resenting the way it was presented to me by my mother and so, kicking a hole in the piano--
How do you kick a hole in a piano?
Well, it was an upright piano.
Okay; you must have had very sturdy shoes.

I had a lot of hate and anger, and you can kick big holes in pianos when you're very angry. That, plus listening to the great composers and really being drawn into music through their great talent, listening to the moderns of the present day and appreciating what they had done, enjoying that, and scratching
along, discovering that I had come across no system or no person that was able to bring knowledge that I required to me so that I could assimilate it.
It was about that time if my memory serves me right that the Schillinger system was very popular, or at least talked about a good deal. Did you ever brush against that?

No. I brushed against the Schillinger system by being associated with other guys that were writing for some of the rehearsal bands that I was writing for, who were using that system, and appreciating the beautiful harmonic changes that the system produced--
Do you remember exactly what it consisted of?
No.

It seems to me, if I remember correctly, that there was a formula, if you wanted a mood of such and such, there were ways that you could refer to the formula and figure out how to get a green mood or a blue mood.
Exactly. And that turned me off.
It was a forerunner of computer music.

Right. I felt that it wasn't a live thing if it didn't grow from its own seed and develop of itself. If it was already created and lying in a drawer to be pulled out and used, I didn't want any part of it, so I avoided the Schillinger system. I took a quick look at it, felt that I understood what it was doing, I appreciated what it was producing; I didn't like the way it was being produced.
Were there other major teaching methods or "systems" in those days that I don't recall?

There was the twelve tone thing that was happening, which I also dug a great deal, but I couldn't find myself following a method of writing, a way of writing. Actually, I can see that in the things I've written, I seem

to utilize all of it. There's songs or passages that I've written that sound straight out of a Schillinger book, there's other stuff I've done that sounds like it came from the twelve tone system; I don't think about these things when I'm writing. I hear what I hear, I try to put it on paper, try to get close to what I hear, and If I don't, whatever I find is a discovery, whether I can use it then or not. At least you're discovering something different, something new. Keep on searching and you'll find different things.
Are you often astonished what you have found, what you have created?
Yes. Many times I'm just shocked by it.

Sometimes I'll write without thinking about the performer--I don't know what I'll be thinking about, it will just come out of me. I'll follow a line with this and follow a line with this and not really have an idea of what they would sound like together, not really caring

and yet when I hear the result I'm overwhelmed and with these things I don't feel that I was the great creator. This is another thing that I tripped into, but thank God by that accident I discovered how to create this particular new thing I found. That's the way I write; that's the way I've always written. I let it pour out of me; whatever. It doesn't always come out right either. I've made all the mistakes that everyone else makes.
Were you conscious of Gershwin's writing, particularly conscious of Gershwin's work in those years?
Yeah.

I understand that he is the Schillinger system. For Porgy and Bess I think he used that and I think that's one of the greatest works I've heard in American music. That opera-- is it considered an opera?
I think it is now, yeah. As a matter of fact, he called it an opera. I've got some of the original sheet music for
that, it was called from an opera, but of course most people in those days thought opera was Italian and richly endowed by the Metropolitan and such, and I'm sure they didn't think of it as an opera.

As I was saying, methods-- I can't get along with methods--not that I can't get along, I can't use them to write with. I can't get a method to come out of me. Nevertheless, I thank God that there was a guy like Schillinger who came along and invented this method so that a guy like Gershwin could come along and use his method to produce Porgy and Bess.
I have speculated-- surely not at length, but if Gershwin had lived which musical direction he would have gone--have you ever speculated, can you imagine what he might be doing musically?
No. I think that would be very difficult, with creative people I don't think you can really call the turn they could go.
The possibilities are limitless. It's impossible to think of directions and then, they could just continue where they were.
What do you think of other Gershwin music, referring to your opinion of Porgy and Bess, what about some of the other Gershwin music?
I think he was a very good writer.
I don't mean the pop music.
You mean the piano things?
Just piano things.
I think he was an excellent writer. An American in Paris, you mean?
Yes.
I think he was very good. I enjoy his work very much.
To leap forward and in exactly the same thing, what do you think of Leonard Bernstein?
I like him, I think he's very good.

I think that his West Side Story was very innovative in terms of songs, in terms of the form of American songs, pop tunes, things that became popular. He didn't hold to the thirty two bars, he didn't hold to the acceptable harmonies.

I'm so delighted that these things have changed and become acceptable, because I remember the battles I used to go through. I had a period of being a songwriter where I wasn't a musician, a jazz player, a jazz writer and orchestrator, a composer; none of those things, just a songwriter with a lyricist as a partner.
What was his name? Segal.
Jack Siegal.
Jack has had a bunch of popular songs, 'When Sunny Gets Blue'.
I would write a song and it was very possible for my song to be eight, seven eight and eight, the form, or it would be eleven

and four and nine--away from the ordinary, and these damn publishers would get on me, you're not sticking to song form; I'd say, so what, do you like it? Yeah, it's nice, but you're not sticking to form. People won't like it, or you don't end in the same key you started in. I said if I had told you--if I hadn't told you that I ended in a different key, would you have known? No. I said, what the hell is the difference? Well, the fact that I know, people won't like it if you end in a different key than you started; because I wrote tunes that started in D say, and ended in A.
What did Slegal think of this?

He went along with me; he accepted all that, but he understood the publishers which I had great trouble--well, understanding was not hard, but accepting it was another thing. I couldn't accept their decisions. Anyway, they pushed me off for years and years, and now they're accepting other
people that are doing it.
Which of your tunes was closest to being a "hit?" "Forgetful," perhaps?

Let me see.
You're talking about songs with lyrics?
That you as George Handy, songwriter.

What was that tune that Ella Mae recorded?
I never had a hit--never. But one or two of my songs made a little money.
Which ones were they?
I'm trying to think of the damn titles.
Were some recorded by bands other than--people other than you were associated with?
A lot of my tunes were recorded by Jo Stafford, Billy Eckstine recorded one of mine. I've had several records of some of the tunes.
Did you decide you wanted to be a songwriter or just found yourself being a songwriter?
It was convenient at the time to become a songwriter. I fancied myself in love with Betty Hutton.
Did she record any of your material?
No, but I wrote some stuff for her, which is in the Paramount archives. They'll probably lay there until the end of time. But no, she never did the stuff.

I came out to Hollywood, we embraced we went back to her place, we went to bed together, professed undying love for each other and in the morning I took her to the plane where she was going on a USO tour and I said goodby sweetheart and she said okay, it will only be six weeks and when I get back we'll be married immediately. I said okay, darling, have a good trip and I'll see you at the altar; that was the last time I saw her, when I put her on the plane.
That was a fast love affair anyway.
Wasn't it?
Never a dull moment.
That brought me out to the coast and that had me leave Raeburn.
That was 1945 or so, I guess?

Right. That was '45. I never saw her again but about six weeks later I got a call from the head of the studio, who said Betty felt pretty badly about things but she couldn't bring herself to come back on the lot and face me, so would I please leave so that their star could come back to the lot in comfort. And without her, in those days, Paramount was up a creek. She was bringing in all the money, she was their big star. That was it, she had a change of heart and couldn't face me. That took me away from Paramount and put me into town where after a few months--
Hal McKusick was living with me at the time--
By into town, you mean back in L.A.?
L.A., I was living in L.A. and I decided to stay there.

(Johnny) Bothwell had had an argument with probably the rest of the band, because he was quite a character and Boyd finally told him he'd have to go and he called McKusick who was living with me, and Hal went and rejoined them, because he had been with them until I pulled him out of the band to come to the coast with me.
To work at Paramount at the studios?
I told him that I could find him work if he came out there with me.

He rejoined them in San Francisco and a few weeks later they called me--Harry Biss who had been playing with them blew his top one night and put his fist through a glass door and cut his arm up so he couldn't play, and that's when it happened. I went back and rejoined the

band and he wanted a chart on "There's No You" and I sat down and I can't tell you what happened but there was a click in my life, something clicked, all the fences went down and I could see, my horizon was limitless, I could write anything I wanted anytime.

As I said, down went the fences and I don't know what else could have been involved in the sudden understanding. I think a great deal of it was my anger at how I had been treated by everyone, the world, people who were supposedly close to me, my loves, my friends; I felt somehow as if I had been brutalized and I resented everything. I resented people telling me you can't do this, you can't do it, it isn't done, people won't understand and I just suddenly said, I can do anything. If I do it it's right; if you don't like it, that's opinion, and they have a right to their opinion, but they do not have the right to tell me I can't do it.
Were you aware of this revelation while you were writing that or
No, it was there before I put the first mark on paper.
Was that a particularly good tune, did you like that tune? Was that helpful?
It was a fine tune, but it wouldn't have mattered what the tune was. I was just ready at that moment; that was the time. That was it, and it was unbelievably easy, to just go on and do it.
Where did you write that, were you in a hotel room?
Right.
On the road?
Right. I was at the Palace Hotel in San Francisco.
From that point on, everything. We're a little out of order, but I'll continue it. Tell me about when you brought the chart down--
(Side B of Tape 2 ended at this point. Transcript will continue in accordance with Tape 3.)
I think they were probably a little surprised; they were. But they were pleased. Everybody was delighted.
It wasn't a particularly difficult chart, you didn't have an awful lot of trouble running it down.
No. I didn't feel that anything was difficult.
What did Boyd think about it?
What could he do? He looked at the expression on the guys' faces and they looked happy; he looked happy. He didn't know.

Boyd--I don't know what justification, other than business, he would have for being an orchestra leader. He was a piss poor musician with not even good taste. I think he went along with everything that was done because
people who he thought knew what was going on dug it. Boyd was number one opportunist; he was smart in that way.
I'm sure he knew he had something; he didn't know what it was, but something was happening right in front of his eyes and he wasn't going to stop it. He let it happen.
Who was managing the band at that point?
At that point there was a guy named Lou--what was his last name--he had a daughter who became a popular singer. I can't think of his last name--Lou something.

He didn't know either, but he also went along with it. They noticed that people were starting to come to our rehearsals, our rehearsals began to look like performances, there were so many people around.
Kenton used to have his rehearsal and at the end of his rehearsal, he'd tell his guys to come down to our rehearsal to listen to what was happening. He said something new is
Did Kenton ask you to write for him?
Yeah. I still have a huge score, I thought I found it last night, but that wasn't it, the last thing I'd written for him, but I never got to him.
For which band?
His concert band.
The 1952 band, the one with the strings?
Right. It was a huge band, a very large band.
Bob Gretinger must have been writing for that band.
Right.
Did you know Bob?
No, I never met him, but I knew of him, I heard his work. He was an
excellent writer.

I assume this is true, it's been told to me and I've forgotten by whom, but someone I respect, Gretinger didn't write on score paper, he wrote on graph paper, he wrote in colored pencil, as I visualized it, something like some of that John Cage devices.
For Schillinger also.
Gretinger may have been a follower of Schillinger, but he wrote on graph paper.
I've never heard that.

He almost took vows of poverty and he would take twenty or thirty dollars a week from Stan and lived in a little room somewhere. Stan tried to give him more money and tried to get him to move into another house to break out of this, but he wanted to live that way. I don't know that, but it was told to me.
I would find no reason
to doubt anything like that; why not. People are different, one from the other.
That might have appealed to him.
As I said, I don't even know Bob, I don't know why he would have done something like that but I could certainly understand that people would do things like that.
What prevented your getting--to get back to the line--what prevented your getting that thing to the Kenton band?
Being sick.
Is it complete?
No, unfinished.

The first movement was complete and the second movement was--I think I was just about finished with the second movement. I may have needed a few more bars I think, but I had two more movements planned. But it was a long work. The first movement ran seven minutes or so.
Could the first two movements be performed independently? Would it
stand? Would you like to have that performed some time?
Where would I find a band that big?
Let me back up and finish off that first--before we get to Boyd, I want to be sure that we made all the notes here--what did you do for Jimmy and Tommy Dorsey?

It was all conversation. For Tommy I wrote one thing and it was a pop tune of the day and you know I can't remember what came of it. Something happened. I told you about this manager that I had that brought grief to me in various ways, the way Dave Dexter used to insult me in print even though he didn't know me, because he had had this physical fist fight with Jerry and Jerry had beaten him up, so naturally Jerry's clients became his number one pet hate and he would write--
What was Jerry's last name?
Brightman, that was the name he was born with, but he changed it to Herbert J. Morrison.
He would write things like Pete Rugulo's the greatest writer I've heard and he doesn't have to wear a beard to be noticed.
Musical criticisms.
Anyway, we were getting at what?
Your work with Dorsey.
Right.

So I had done this chart for Dorsey, I had done a thing for Benny Goodman and a thing for Dorsey at the same time and Jerry was to deliver my scores and pick up the money, and he brought the thing in to Benny and told me they went through it and Benny looked puzzled but gave him the check. I got a letter from Mel Powell regarding that score about a year later saying that the score--
(Tape went blank for a few seconds)
--there was some fast work with clarinet and piano between Benny and
Mel and Mel indicated in his letter that when he came to those passages Benny would just look at his part instead of playing it, while Mel was playing his part.
He ran through the chart, paid for it; I never heard it, and that was the end of the chart for Benny.
Were the passages difficult for him or just puzzling?
I wouldn't think so. I have no idea.
I thought he could play anything.
I think he can; I don't understand why that happened, but that's what happened, as reported to me.

Now the chart that went to Dorsey, I don't even know whether he ran it down. He paid for it, but he was angry and the reason he was angry was that he had heard that I told people that he offered to make me another Sy Oliver if I would come and write for him, and I didn't do
And that made Sy mad?
It made Tommy mad.
Sy was presumably yelling to Tommy about that, I should imagine?

I really don't know whether it got to Sy. I can't think of why it wouldn't have, but I didn't say anything like that. I'm not the kind of a person that makes snotty remarks about people. I don't do that. But Tommy was upset about that and when I heard that he was upset, I said well, that's life. If he's upset, let him be upset.
I might as well ask it on camera, we were going over the list of the people you had worked for before Raeburn, cleaning up that area of history, and commenting on such.
On the back of one of my albums is a list of the bands I had been with,
Is that the same list there?
Incidentally, the names of the tunes that were recorded by Ella Mae Moss (Morse) there, what are the names?
"Rip Van Winkle".
That made me some money. You're asking which came close to being a hit, I guess that would be it because it was in the movie, I heard about.
What movie?
Something with Jane Withers and in the picture, Jane Withers sang the tune.
Like everything else I find out about my music, someone told me they saw the picture and she sang it.
You didn't get a magnificent check for use in the movies?
I recall no magnificent check, but that particular tune did make me more
money than the others. I had a few records on it.
Three people did "Where You At", Bobby Troup, Dave and Jimmy and Gary Trio.
Right.
That's been bringing in money in dribs and drabs.
"You Were Loved So Well", Jo Stafford did.
That was never released.
I don't remember the tune; have I ever heard the tune?
Probably not.
I'm sure it's not on any of the Raeburn material.
No, I never wrote it for the Raeburn band. I was about to.
"If Love Is Trouble", Eckstine recorded that.
I don't know that tune either. "Forgetful", somebody told me--
that's a Johnny Carson lead-in--somebody told me, that you had a dog named Forgetful.
No I didn't.

That was one of my manager's creations. He set up a picture shooting session for me and they came to my house and I was close friends with the Dead End Kids in those days and Gabe Rodell was visiting me on the day that they were shooting the pictures and Gabe came over his dog, so they put Gabe's dog into the picture with me and they said George Handy sitting at home with his dog, Forgetful.
That's the story of my dog, Forgetful.
That was good.
I never had a dog.
That was a good press agent stunt, because Forgetful would be a lovely name for a puppy.
It wasn't true.
So many good stories aren't.
What did you do with Artie Shaw?
I played with him for about a month, I guess, in San Diego, at one point. Dodo was his regular pianist, but Dodo was ill.
I saw that band in Chicago with Dodo on it, but Chuck Gentry was playing and Herbie Steward.
Right. So that's how that happened, I worked with him for a month.
You didn't record for the band?
No.

We were starting to talk about certain things. He wanted me to talk Boyd into letting him use the band--our band, that he would take our band out and call it the Artie Shaw Band, but to play our stuff.
That would be somewhat confusing, wouldn't it?
I didn't do it. I told him I didn't think anybody would go for it. But
This is after the band had already established itself musically?
Yeah. Right in that period of being established. There was a lot of talk about the band at the time.
I couldn't understand why he would want it? To play his book I could understand. Or to have you write a new book for him, or something like that. No, I don't understand it either.
He was always a pretty impetuous man.
Exactly.
That was the time when he was with Ava Gardner, when I played with him.
Was that a day-to-day hassle with him?
Tell me about Shaw, your reactions to him.
I just felt that he seemed to be a guy that was amused by everything.
as if he was standing off looking at the world like he had inside information about everything.
Was he easy to get on with?
I had no problem with him at all.
Was it a happy band?
Yes.

Most of the guys had known each other for years, not as a result of playing with that band, most of the guys had worked together in a lot of bands; they were real close and for that reason, they were a happy band.
I didn't pay any attention to the beefs--there were a few beefs, but I can't recall what they were. Generally speaking, it was a content band. He was paying good money, that was for sure.
That band was very successful, that was one of his really successful periods; wasn't it?
Right.
That's even more along the lines why I was so puzzled by his request; I couldn't understand it at all, but that's what he wanted to do.
Shaw had money of his own; didn't he? Wasn't he of some wealth?
I had heard the rumors that he came from a wealthy family, but of my own knowledge I have no idea.
What did you do with Freddie Slack, anything of any real significance?
A few charts, played on the road with him.
Were you a boogie-woogie piano player?
No, he did the boogie-woogie.
Other than those particular things, I played and he would front.
He didn't front the band from the piano then?
No.
I didn't know that.
He stood out in front.
Ella Mae was on that band, wasn't she?

Right. This wasn't the original band that she had done the 'Cow Cow Boogie' with; this was years later when she was an established star on her own, and she was the star of the show and the band, for the show, happened to be Freddie Slack.
I see.
But she wasn't singing with the band, she was the number one headline. His band had the show, and she was my sister-in-law.

When you first ran into Raeburn, at that point Eddie was writing for the band, the first phase, and who else; do you remember who had contributed some stuff? Harry Klee wrote some things, it seems to me.
Harry Klee?
Yeah.
The flutist?
Yeah.
I didn't know that Harry wrote.
I think his name is on "Boyd's Nest". I may be wrong about that, but I believe his name is on top of "Boyd's Nest."
Not as the writer.
It's up there.
This comes as a shock to me right now. I had no idea that Harry could write, much less that he wrote that.
I'll look at it carefully when I get home; I certainly won't vouch for it because a lot of that stuff I haven't looked at for a while.
It could have been a sax solo by Harry Klee and maybe that part got left out.
No, this is on each
of the parts. Maybe Junior was there. Anyway, Finkle wrote most of that book, I guess.
I think so, at that time. I don't know who the other guys were that he was using. The only one that I was aware of was Ed Finkle.
How did you run into Boyd at the beginning?

I was introduced to him by Jerry, the manager. I explained to you how my friend Jack Siegel--he wasn't my friend then, I didn't know him either, I was introduced to Jack as the writer of the song called 'Who Started Love' and he needed to get his song into Boyd's library because Boyd had a wire out of the hotel and Jack wanted to get his song on the air. The way to do it was to get somebody to write an arrangement to give to Boyd, and so, I don't recall exactly, but I think probably Jack paid for it, rather than Boyd, and that's how Boyd and I met, as the
arranger of Jack's song. Boyd was impressed with the chart and asked me if I would like to write for the band, and that's how it began. After a little while, I joined the band on piano.
Do you remember what you wrote in those days, any of the material?
It would be difficult to recall.
Nothing that has survived into this library?
There was a thing--I wrote a thing for Trummy Young to sing on our theater tour, which was "Is You Is Or Is You Ain't My Baby"; I recall that one.
I imagine there were a whole bunch of nondescript pop tunes, publisher's material that came through in the early days that I wrote, but I don't really remember those things.
That was essentially a sort of a gray or non-important part of the career. You were just writing pop tunes and
playing piano?
Right.
The piano playing must have been notable now and then. You were still you.
Yeah, yeah.

In those days I had a kind of self confidence that I don't think was really too genuine. Deep inside of me I didn't enjoy my piano playing and so I couldn't take compliments as being genuine and that's the way it's been most of the time.
The band didn't record anything during that period, did it?
No.
There were some dates but I don't remember them recording anything of mine.
The first release, as we go through this thing,--the first release, 1944, was "Starlight Avenue", "I Dream Of You", "This Must Be Love" and "It Could Happen To You".
Those are, I guess, pre-you.
Right. I don't even know if any of those are Fink's either.
As a matter of fact, you were on the band. I'm not aware of your writing any of those things.
No, I didn't.
The next was December 1944, was a series of V discs, and that date included "Two Spoos", "Tunesia," "Who Started Love," "Key F,"--
Key F?
K-E-Y, capital F. "Grey Suede," "Barefoot Boy With Cheek," which I think was "Barefoot Boyd With Cheek,"--
"Gray Suede?"
"Gray Suede." 1944.
I'd love to get a copy of that. I'm trying to find good copies of some of that stuff.
I've got a copy of "Gray Suede" on order.
In good condition?
A new one, there's a new pressing of it. It's that Jubilee.
Who's releasing that?
One of the pirates.
I think it's that Florida company.

I'll tell you, I've got the name and address. I've got a catalog at home.
And these guys are re-leasing "Key F" and "Gray Suede?"

No.

Yeah. A big black guy was the thing.*

How the hell can they

Hindsight Records.

When you're down next month-- I really wish I knew how to do this properly, get after all these

I heard one cut out of it, I never heard the whole album.
I have it; I'll play it for you.

How did that happen, you didn't have a contract with them?

All four of them are there?

You were there and allowed it.

I don't think I'm capable of handling that, simply because I don't know. I'm not a good jazz historian at all, and for a great period of my life I didn't pay attention, I wasn't involved constantly. I was just involved at small moments in time, although I
managed to keep working through that time; still I wasn't looking around, I didn't notice who else was on the scene, didn't listen to what else was being done and I wasn't interested.
I'm learning in these last few years what went on. I'm discovering things that people are astounded I didn't know.
For example?
Some of the new people that I wasn't aware of, some of the things that had been recorded that I wasn't aware of.
I was looking through your records, which I guess is bad manners, like going through a bookcase, you've got a lot of Keith Jarrett there.
I love the way he plays. He stimulates me; he really opens the doors too. He opens them for me, baby, just the way I hope I open them for other people. This kid really is an astonishing musician.
Who else is astonishing currently?
I don't know. I haven't really heard anybody else of the players that I think are astonishing.
We haven't talked much about singers.
I don't think I know too much about singers. I haven't really worked with many of the great singers, people that I like.
Who are the ones you like?
Now I'm going to say David Allen, right?
You better say David Allen.
I like the way David sings. There are some people I like, but I tell you, I'm losing strength in my head, man. I'm getting tired.
(Tape ended at this point. Interview concluded.)

segments.title: Growing up in Brooklyn over his father's ether-filled practice
segments.summary: Schremp opens the interview; Handy was born in Brooklyn, his father a doctor doing ear operations, which inspired the title 'Tonsillectomy'.

segments.title: His mother the pianist and her daily practice
segments.summary: His mother practiced the same pieces daily for a concert that never came, and he could tell lunch by the music; his father liked music but was not musical.

segments.title: Mother's brutal teaching and his resentment of teachers
segments.summary: His mother taught him miserably until he kicked a hole in the piano; he quit music for years and came to resent every teacher, learning instead from other musicians.

segments.title: Returning to the keyboard and discovering the moderns
segments.summary: He returned to music on his own terms, exploring sounds at the keyboard and listening to Stravinsky, Ravel and Bartok before going back to Bach and Mozart.

segments.title: First job at a Long Beach hotel
segments.summary: At fourteen or fifteen a neighbor saxophonist got him a summer job as pianist in a kid band, which his mother opposed and his father allowed.

segments.title: Neighborhood bands and the failed medical future
segments.summary: He formed kid bands, still assumed he would be a doctor, until fainting while watching his father operate ended the idea.

segments.title: Chops, 'bullshitting' and resenting being taught
segments.summary: He describes his facility for making things sound right while improvising, as in forgetting a Mozart movement, and ties it to resentment of structure.

segments.title: Writing from the start, and the violinist uncle
segments.summary: He began composing as soon as he returned to music, writing violin and piano pieces for his uncle, whose professional acceptance meant more than family praise.

segments.title: A bad year at Juilliard
segments.summary: Juilliard was his first formal music school; he skipped for the movies and found the classical students hostile to jazz.

segments.title: The order of schools: NYU pre-med, Copland, Juilliard, back to NYU
segments.summary: He sorts out the sequence of NYU pre-med, Copland, Juilliard and NYU music courses, being asked to leave most of them.

segments.title: Studying with Aaron Copland
segments.summary: His mother found Copland for him; Copland only asked for melodies and gave his opinions, so Handy wrote them on the train to lessons.

segments.title: Later meeting with Copland and leaving his lessons
segments.summary: He met Copland years later at a Brooklyn Museum concert, reflects on whether Copland was serious as a teacher, and recalls quitting.

segments.title: Playing ball and Allie Sherman
segments.summary: Talk of his love of sports leads to his friendship with his brother's friend Allie Sherman.

segments.title: Back to NYU downtown and composition with Marion Bauer
segments.summary: After Juilliard he took courses at NYU's downtown school and studied composition with Marion Bauer, again rejecting opinions as teaching.

segments.title: Playing a jazz concert with Gene Krupa at NYU
segments.summary: Krupa came to NYU for a jazz concert and Handy and a clarinetist were found to play with him; later Krupa did not remember him.

segments.title: His own jazz piano and who he listened to
segments.summary: He calls himself a below-average jazz pianist, describes the 'oompa' style and listening to Wilson, Stacy, Waller and Tatum, and bands rather than writers.

segments.title: Choosing writing over playing; first paid chart for Richard Himber
segments.summary: He realized he preferred writing, and describes writing his first paid arrangement for Himber for very little money.

segments.title: Joining the Raymond Scott band
segments.summary: At twenty he won an audition as Raymond Scott's pianist and admired Scott's courage to be different.

segments.title: Writing for Scott, manager Harvey Bacall and the ten-dollar bonus
segments.summary: On tour Handy wrote charts for Dorothy Collins and others, was paid ten dollars extra by manager Harvey Bacall, and left over it.

segments.title: Programmatic titles and humor and anger in his music
segments.summary: His titles came with pictured stories, and he finds his music both humorous and angry.

segments.title: The razzer in 'Bloos' and Barry Ulanov's 'Dadaism' objection
segments.summary: At the Norman Granz session Ulanov stopped the recording over a drum razzer, calling it Dadaism, so Handy substituted a contrabassoon.

segments.title: Himber and Scott compared; Michael Loring's band
segments.summary: They compare the Himber and Scott bands, then Handy lists Michael Loring's large pop band, Chester and Spanier.

segments.title: Bob Chester's band and Starburst
segments.summary: Schremp asks about Bob Chester's band and theme; Handy remembers a decent, easygoing leader from a wealthy Detroit family.

segments.title: Joining Jack Teagarden and the 'Professor' arrangements
segments.summary: After the army he spent about a year touring the South with Teagarden, who loved his 'Body and Soul' chart and called him the Professor.

segments.title: The Mobile hotel brawl with Jack and Addie Teagarden
segments.summary: Addie smashed a whiskey bottle across Jack's face, and Jack still played the show bandaged.

segments.title: Playing what you can think of, and Boyd's performers
segments.summary: A Teagarden quote leads Handy to say he is not tough on players, and Schremp asks about Boyd's performances of his pieces.

segments.title: Tape trouble and drafted into the army
segments.summary: Schremp mentions re-doing a lost portion of the interview; Handy was drafted around September 1942 and served months at Camp Gruber.

segments.title: Writing a book for Herbie Fields's band
segments.summary: Back in uniform he met Herbie Fields and manager Pete Cameron and wrote a book for a band that never took off.

segments.title: Pricing charts for Lionel Hampton
segments.summary: Hampton wanted four or five charts, but his agent rejected Handy's hundred-dollar price, ending the job.

segments.title: Arranger or composer, and his insecurity as a jazz soloist
segments.summary: He saw himself as a composer, felt he lacked ease in swinging time, and wrote 'Foolish Little Boy' for Dodo Marmarosa.

segments.title: Not writing solos for himself; comping and getting hung up
segments.summary: He avoids writing himself as soloist, comps well, but freezes when soloing.

segments.title: Hypnosis and playing better
segments.summary: They discuss hypnosis as an aid to playing; Handy tried hypnotherapy but says he was never hypnotized.

segments.title: Litter bearer in the army, and the tuba
segments.summary: Handy was a litter bearer, got a band transfer he no longer wanted, then took the tuba after a heel spur ended his service.

segments.title: Life before the army, sports and what pleased him
segments.summary: His life then was not all music; he loved sports and weighed ball playing against music.

segments.title: Distance from the army band and fear of litter work
segments.summary: He never got close to the army band musicians and admits he feared litter work; he had wanted the Air Force or tanks.

segments.title: Teagarden's big band and the drunken trumpeter Stirling Bose
segments.summary: He recalls the personnel of Teagarden's band and Jack leaving drunken trumpeter Stirling on the road.

segments.title: Drinking on the bands
segments.summary: He started drinking in the Scott band, and some musicians could still perform while others could not; Teagarden's wife managed the band.

segments.title: Summary of his musical life before Boyd
segments.summary: He sums up his pre-Boyd years: told he would be a doctor, his mother's teaching, listening to the moderns, and finding no teacher.

segments.title: Why he avoided the Schillinger system
segments.summary: He sampled Schillinger through other writers, liked the harmonies but disliked a prefabricated method.

segments.title: Twelve-tone, method-free writing and discovery
segments.summary: He writes what he hears without a system and is often astonished by the results.

segments.title: Gershwin and Porgy and Bess
segments.summary: He admires Porgy and Bess, thanks Schillinger for enabling it, and declines to guess Gershwin's later direction.

segments.title: Other Gershwin, and Bernstein's West Side Story
segments.summary: He enjoys Gershwin's piano works and praises West Side Story for breaking song forms.

segments.title: Songwriting with Jack Siegal and publishers' objections to form
segments.summary: With lyricist Jack Siegal he wrote songs in odd forms that publishers disliked, and a few made small money.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: Betty Hutton, Hollywood and leaving Raeburn
segments.summary: He went to Hollywood for Betty Hutton, who left him within weeks, and stayed in Los Angeles.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: Rejoining Boyd Raeburn and the breakthrough on 'There's No You'
segments.summary: Returning when Harry Biss was hurt, writing 'There's No You' he felt all limits fall away.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: Boyd's reaction, and the band's manager Lou
segments.summary: Boyd let the new music happen while knowing little; the manager Lou also went along.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: Kenton's rehearsal crowd and Handy's unfinished score; Bob Gretinger
segments.summary: Kenton told his players to hear Raeburn's rehearsals; Handy started a large concert score for Kenton but fell ill, and they discuss Bob Gretinger.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: Charts for Tommy Dorsey and Benny Goodman, and Dave Dexter
segments.summary: He tells of charts for Goodman and Dorsey, Benny's puzzlement, Tommy's anger, and manager Jerry Brightman's feud with Dave Dexter.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: His recorded songs: 'Rip Van Winkle' and others
segments.summary: He lists songs recorded by Ella Mae Morse, Bobby Troup, Jo Stafford and Eckstine and what they earned.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: The dog named Forgetful
segments.summary: The press story of his dog Forgetful was a photo-shoot invention using a friend's dog.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: A month with Artie Shaw
segments.summary: Handy subbed for Dodo in Shaw's band in San Diego, and Shaw asked him to get Boyd's band to play under Shaw's name.

segments.chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
segments.title: Playing with Freddie Slack
segments.summary: He wrote a few charts and played piano for Slack's band, backing his sister-in-law Ella Mae Morse.

segments.title: Who wrote Raeburn's early book: Harry Klee and Eddie Finckel
segments.summary: Schremp asks who wrote for the first Raeburn band; Handy knew mainly Finckel.

segments.title: Meeting Boyd and his first Raeburn writing
segments.summary: Jack Siegel's song led to arranging for Boyd and joining on piano; he recalls early pop charts and 'Is You Is'.

segments.title: Early Raeburn records, V-discs, Jubilee and pirate reissues
segments.summary: Schremp lists the 1944 sessions and the Jubilee broadcast, and Handy objects to unauthorised reissues.

segments.title: Royalties lost: the Zoot Sims album and Buck Hill
segments.summary: He got nothing from the Zoot Sims album; Schremp tells how little record royalties pay.

segments.title: The 'jazz symphony' Jubilee broadcast
segments.summary: He was unaware the rehearsal was a live broadcast; four pieces were billed as a symphony.

segments.title: Pieces relabeled as a suite
segments.summary: He resents others relabeling his pieces as a suite.

segments.title: Why he left the band: Betty Hutton and the Paramount contract
segments.summary: He left for Betty Hutton and the plan to write songs with Jack Segal, leading to contracts with Paramount and Capitol.

segments.title: Staff songwriter at Paramount and Hollywood's slow pace
segments.summary: On staff pay of about a thousand a week he disliked Hollywood's slow tempo, since he needs each piece resolved.

segments.title: Dating his Paramount time against Boris Morros and the Raeburn records
segments.summary: They try to fix dates, Handy conducted the Jubilee date while Ike Carpenter played piano.

segments.title: Idle days in Hollywood
segments.summary: He played ball in the park, learned that nobody goes to the office, and mistook downtown Los Angeles for Hollywood.

segments.title: The flood of new writing: Gray Suede, Key F and Dalvatore
segments.summary: Once the block lifted the pieces poured out, and he regrets that others turned them into suites.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Substitute pianists and Joe Albany
segments.summary: He stayed off tours, using Ike, Dodo or Joe Albany, a gifted but troubled pianist.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Boyd Raeburn as a saxophonist
segments.summary: Handy found Boyd a horrible saxophonist who played every reed instrument for show.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Boyd's society-band origins and other leaders turning to jazz
segments.summary: Schremp tells Boyd's background and how hotel bandleaders moved toward jazz in the war years.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Things happened to Boyd: the Washington players and Eddie Finckel
segments.summary: Boyd never caused anything; the band turned jazz-oriented through the Washington players hired in its society days.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Singer David Allyn
segments.summary: Handy loved David Allyn, who hopes to come back east and sing with him.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Ginnie Powell's interference and her singing of Handy's charts
segments.summary: Handy describes how Ginnie Powell pushed Boyd to change personnel and took the singer's job before marrying Boyd.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Frankie Socolow, Hy Mandel and what made the band great
segments.summary: He praises Socolow and says the band was great though some players were weak.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Raeburn alumni: Kluger, Savitt, Benny Harris, Trummy Young, Diz and Bird
segments.summary: Handy recalls trumpet section players and stars like Gillespie and Parker who passed through.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Oscar Pettiford, the Commodore, and Roy Eldridge sitting in
segments.summary: They recall Pettiford and the hotel, and Roy Eldridge sat in after hearing the radio.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Johnny Bothwell's deliberately corny solo
segments.summary: Bothwell played a tasty solo on purpose to prove how corny the band's taste was.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Bothwell's missed Basie job and lost library
segments.summary: Schremp says Bothwell was asked to join Basie but could not tour the South as a white lead alto; his library was lost.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Bothwell the strange, handsome leader of the band
segments.summary: Handy describes Bothwell's chicken-like Hodges imitation and the rift in the band.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Groupies
segments.summary: Girls followed bands from town to town even then.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: The Raeburn audience
segments.summary: The audience depended on venue; Handy imagines Kenton's crowd plus more.

segments.chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
segments.title: Hostile Southern audiences and the absence of black players on tour
segments.summary: Audiences in the South and Southwest were hostile, and black stars joined only in the north; Trummy Young stayed longest.

segments.title: The Club Morocco and later New York troubles
segments.summary: The band settled at the Club Morocco for about three months; Schremp mentions its later sparse New York audiences.

segments.title: The last night he played with the band
segments.summary: Handy filled in for a drunk Dodo for an air shot at the Morocco, his last time playing with Raeburn.

segments.title: The planned Capitol-style session and Max Steiner's 'Over the Rainbow'
segments.summary: The planned session of his new pieces yielded only 'Dalvatore' and half of 'Over the Rainbow'; Johnny Richards may have finished it.

segments.title: The salary dispute that ended his time with Boyd
segments.summary: A loan with promised salary was not honored by Boyd and his backer, so Handy said goodbye.

segments.title: Johnny Richards waiting to take over
segments.summary: Handy suspects they lined up Richards to replace him but does not blame Richards.

segments.title: Which bands were really innovative: Bobby Sherwood and George Barnes
segments.summary: Schremp names Kenton, Herman and Raeburn as the three adventurous bands; Handy dismisses Sherwood's claim.

segments.title: How Kenton and Herman made it work while Raeburn did not
segments.summary: Schremp asks why leaders like Herman and Kenton succeeded; Handy says he has no right to judge Kenton.

segments.title: Ben Pollack's record misrepresented the band
segments.summary: Handy says the Pollack release gave listeners something else than the band's real music, and Boyd let it happen.

segments.title: Johnny Richards as a writer
segments.summary: They sort out what Richards contributed and Handy calls him a marvelous but different writer.

segments.title: How Handy met Johnny Richards over 'Bahia'; the Neophonics
segments.summary: Handy phoned Richards after hearing 'Bahia'; Schremp explains Joel Kaye's Neophonics.

segments.title: Looking back: a free hand with Raeburn
segments.summary: Handy says it was an exciting time with a free hand to write and he would let himself write again.

segments.title: Boyd's name on the arrangements
segments.summary: Boyd stamped his name on arrangements, and a story tells of a pitiful chart he wrote himself.

segments.title: Cut loose from the band and drifting to New York
segments.summary: The Raeburn years were fun with later knotted stomachs; Handy went home and then to New York, where trouble began.

segments.title: Curiosity about heroin
segments.summary: He overcame his fear out of curiosity, with friends doing it around him.

segments.title: First experience with opium and heroin in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Two Shaw sidemen offered him opium; he sat stoned for fifteen hours and tried heroin about six months later.

segments.title: Eighteen years addicted
segments.summary: He did not know he could get dependent; it interfered with his creativity for eighteen years.

segments.title: The 1950s albums and chronology
segments.summary: He lists the flute sonata, quartets, the New York suite, 'By George' and 'Handyland, U.S.A.'

segments.title: How the second Label X album came about
segments.summary: Jerry Brightman set it up after Handy took over a date, and he designed a one-of-each band.

segments.title: Clear music out of pain, and the Birdland engagement
segments.summary: The pristine music was written out of pain; he took the band to Birdland for two weeks opposite Basie.

segments.title: The dream of four Zoots
segments.summary: He dreamed four Zoot Sims playing a solo in harmony, which inspired the altos album.

segments.title: Recording the four-altos album with Zoot Sims
segments.summary: Zoot recorded free choruses, then Handy wrote harmony parts and Zoot overdubbed them.

segments.title: Zoot Sims as a person
segments.summary: He calls Zoot a gentle, great musician and friend.

segments.title: Did Les Paul multitrack before this?
segments.summary: They argue when Les Paul's multitrack recordings were made.

segments.title: Zoot's yearly phone calls
segments.summary: Zoot calls him drunk and tearful, and an album on soprano never happens.

segments.title: 'Bloos' for Norman Granz's Jazz Scene
segments.summary: Written in 1947-48 and released years later, it was one side of Granz's carte blanche album.

segments.title: Instrumentation and form of 'Bloos'
segments.summary: He chose bassoon, contrabassoon, violin and three cellos to collect the essences of blues.

segments.title: Dropping out of sight and the Catskills job
segments.summary: After 1955 little work remained; he came to the Catskills in 1968.

segments.title: Rebuilding his reputation with Elaine's help
segments.summary: As an ex-addict with a bad reputation he started over with scale gigs and settled in the mountains.

segments.title: Musicians who stayed clean now using heroin
segments.summary: He notes that studio players who avoided drugs are now using it.

segments.title: His children
segments.summary: He talks about his children from Flo and their distance from him.

segments.title: The trombonist and bass trumpeter who left for New York
segments.summary: Handy praises a trombonist, probably Johnny Mandel, who left to join the bebop movement.

segments.title: The Ross Russell book and Charlie Parker
segments.summary: He denies the book's story of an argument with Parker over a Coast date.

segments.title: Best and meanest things said about him
segments.summary: He is happiest when people enjoy his writing.

segments.title: Closing questions about the Raeburn period
segments.summary: Schremp asks what Handy would add; he thinks the Raeburn period is covered.

segments.title: Unplayable pianos and the West End Casino summer
segments.summary: At a New Jersey summer job the piano was unplayable, so Boyd gave him the summer off with pay.

segments.title: Out-of-tune pianos, the Rhodes and the Yamaha electric piano
segments.summary: Pianos are poorly kept; he finds the Rhodes decent and a Yamaha closest to acoustic.

segments.title: Commercial hotel work in 1980
segments.summary: He plays accompaniment six nights a week and says he has paid his dues twice.

segments.title: He is no jazz historian
segments.summary: He declines to name high points of jazz, having not paid attention for much of his life.

segments.title: Keith Jarrett, singers and the end of the tape
segments.summary: He loves Jarrett's playing and singer David Allyn, then tires; the tape ends.
